paragraphs.heading: Matter we cannot see
paragraphs.text: Dark matter is a hypothetical kind of matter that does not interact with light or any other electromagnetic radiation, so it is invisible. We infer it from gravity: in many places, things pull and move as if far more matter were present than we can observe. Those places include how galaxies form and change, gravitational lensing, the motion of galaxies inside clusters, and the cosmic microwave background.

paragraphs.heading: Most of the matter there is
paragraphs.text: In the standard Lambda-CDM model of cosmology, the universe's mass and energy is 68.2% dark energy, 26.8% dark matter and just 5% ordinary matter. That makes dark matter about 85% of all the matter. It is thought to act as a gravitational scaffold for cosmic structure. After the Big Bang it gathered into blobs along thin filaments, forming a cosmic web on scales where whole galaxies look like specks.

paragraphs.heading: Thin close to home
paragraphs.text: Dark matter is dense in the halo around a galaxy, but near us it is sparse. In the Solar System its density is much lower than that of normal matter. Gather up every bit of it out to Neptune's orbit and you would have around 10¹⁷ kg, similar to one large asteroid. Because it seems to touch ordinary matter only through gravity, catching it in a laboratory is very hard.

paragraphs.heading: What could it be
paragraphs.text: The leading idea is an undiscovered subatomic particle, such as a weakly interacting massive particle (WIMP) or an axion. The other main option is primordial black holes. A minority of astrophysicists instead argue for changing the laws of gravity, with ideas such as modified Newtonian dynamics (MOND). So far no modified gravity theory explains every observation at once, which suggests some dark matter would be needed anyway.

paragraphs.heading: Zwicky weighs a cluster
paragraphs.text: In 1933 the astrophysicist Fritz Zwicky studied the Coma Cluster of galaxies. He estimated its mass from how fast galaxies near its edge were moving, then compared that with an estimate from its brightness and its number of galaxies. The motions implied about 400 times more mass than could be seen, and the visible galaxies could not supply enough gravity for orbits that fast. He concluded that unseen matter, which he called dunkle Materie, was holding the cluster together.

paragraphs.heading: Old numbers, right idea
paragraphs.text: Zwicky's figures were off by more than a factor of ten, mostly because he used an outdated value of the Hubble constant. Even so, he was right that most of the matter pulling by gravity was dark. Unlike scientists today, though, he pictured it as ordinary matter that simply gave off no light. The idea of dark matter only really took hold in the 1970s, when several lines of evidence were put together to argue that galaxies sit inside halos of unseen matter.
